patient_note_history:
History:
HPI: A 21-year-old G1P1 female complains of right lower abdominal pain that started this morning. The pain is severe, crampy, nonradiating, and constant. It is exacerbated by movement and accompanied by fever, nausea, vomiting, and loose stools. The patient noticed some brownish spotting this morning. No urinary symptoms; no abnormal vaginal discharge.
OB/GYN: LMP 5 weeks ago. Regular periods every 4 weeks lasting 7 days. Menarche at age 13. Uncomplicated NSVD at full term 3 years ago.
ROS: Negative except as above.
Allergies: NKDA.
Medications: Ibuprofen.
PMH: STD 6 months ago, possibly treated with ceftriaxone and doxycycline. ("Dr. gave a shot and some pills for a week.")
PSH: No.
SH: 1 pack per day for 6 years, 2-3 beers/week, no illicit drugs. Unprotected sex with multiple partners over the past year.

Diagnosis #3: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy 

History Finding(s): 
- Last menstrual period 5 weeks ago and spotting

- Pain is exacerbated by movement 
- Nausea and vomiting 
- Pain is of recent onset 

Physical Exam Finding(s): 
- RLQ rebound tenderness 
- RLQ guarding
gold_additional_diagnosis:
• Ruptured ovarian cyst: The patient's sudden onset, unilateral lower abdominal pain, rebound tenderness, and guarding are consistent with this diagnosis. Rupture may occur at any time during the menstrual cycle, and symptoms may resemble a ruptured ectopic pregnancy as described above. However, this diagnosis is less common than appendicitis and PID. In addition, given the patient's history of having her last menstrual period 5 weeks ago, ruptured ectopic pregnancy must be placed higher on the differential, as a ruptured ovarian cyst would not be associated with a late menstrual period.

• Adnexal torsion: This presentation may be due to adnexal torsion, an uncommon complication that is most often associated with ovarian enlargement due to a benign mass.

• Gastroenteritis: Viral gastroenteritis presents with crampy abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, low-grade fever, and diarrhea. It can be difficult to distinguish from appendicitis and gynecologic etiologies but is less likely in this case given the presence of rebound tenderness.

• Abortion: The fact that the patient's last menstrual period was only 5 weeks ago makes this diagnosis less likely, but the crampy abdominal pain and vaginal spotting may signal an abortion. Furthermore, the presence of fever suggests possible septic abortion.

• Endometriosis: This is an unlikely diagnosis, in part because the patient has no history of chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, or infertility, which are often associated. In the setting of established endometriosis, this presentation in a patient with acute, severe pain, including rebound tenderness, could be due to rupture of an endometrioma ("chocolate cyst").
raw_opening:
Opening Scenario:

Jessica Anderson, a 21-year-old female, comes to the ED complaining of abdominal pain.

Vital Signs:

BP: 120/80 mm Hg
Temp: 100.5°F (38.1°C)
RR: 20/minute
HR: 88/minute, regular

Examinee Tasks:

1. Take a focused history.
2. Perform a focused physical exam (do not perform rectal, genitourinary, or female breast exam).
3. Explain your clinical impression and workup plan to the patient.
4. Write the patient note after leaving the room.

Checklist/SP Sheet:

Patient Description:

Patient is a 21-year-old female, single with one child.

Notes for the SP:

- Exhibit right lower abdominal tenderness on palpation.
- Show rebound tenderness (pain when the examinee removes their palpating hand).
- Demonstrate guarding (contraction of the abdominal muscles when palpating the RLQ).
- Experience pain in the RLQ when the examinee presses on the RLQ (Rovsing sign).
- Manifest pain when the examinee extends their right hip (psoas sign).

Challenging Questions to Ask:

- "My child is home alone. I need to go now."
- "I can't bear the hospital costs. Please provide a prescription for antibiotics so I can discharge myself."

Examinee Response:

"Ms. Anderson, I understand your concern for your child's safety. It is essential to ensure that your condition does not pose a threat to life.. Our social worker would be happy to work with you to ensure that your child is taken care of, as well as to address any financial concerns you may have."

Examinee Checklist:

Entrance:
- The examinee knocked on the door before entering.
- The examinee made eye contact with the SP.
- The examinee correctly used the patient's name.
- The examinee introduced themselves by name.
- The examinee identified his/her role or position.

Reflective Listening:
- The examinee asked an open-ended question and actively listened to the response.
- The examinee asked the SP to list his/her concerns and listened to the response without interrupting.
- The examinee summarized the SP's concerns, often using the SP's own words.

Information Gathering:
- Examinee elicited data efficiently and accurately.

Connecting With the Patient:
- Examinee recognized the SP's emotions and responded with PEARLS.

Sample Closure:

"Ms. Anderson, your symptoms could stem from an issue with your reproductive system, such as a fallopian tube infection or an ovarian cyst.. They could also stem from a complicated pregnancy, suggested by a positive result on your pregnancy test.. Another possibility is an infection in your appendix, which could require surgery. To ensure an accurate diagnosis, we will need to run some tests, including a blood test, a urinalysis, a pregnancy test, and possibly a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis. We will also need to perform rectal and pelvic exams. Since cigarette smoking is associated with a variety of diseases, I advise you to quit smoking. We offer various options to assist you if you are interested.. I also recommend that you use a condom every time you have intercourse to prevent STDs, including HIV, and to avoid pregnancy. Our social worker is available to meet with you to review your social circumstances and provide various resources.. Do you have any questions for me?"
